Imagine a giant forest where every tree is a page you can visit. That\'s the web! And web pages are written in a language called HTML.
The web is a network of pages connected by links. Every page you\'ve ever visited is built with HTML — the structure language of the web.
Web pages are documents structured with HTML, styled with CSS, and made interactive with JavaScript. We start with HTML — the document skeleton.
HTML uses little labels called tags, like <h1>. Tags tell the page what each thing is — a title, a picture, or a story.

HTML uses tags like

and

to mark up content. Most tags open and close:

Hello

.

Tags are paired markers:

…

. The browser parses them into a tree of elements (the DOM).
In the next lesson you\'ll write your first tag and grow a real plant in your biome. Let\'s go!
Next up: writing your first heading tag and growing your biome.
Next: author your first element and validate it in the live preview.
Write an <h1> and watch it sprout
A heading is the biggest, proudest text on a page — like a tree shouting its name! We write it with the <h1> tag.
Headings give a page its title. <h1> is the most important heading on the page.
<h1> is the top-level heading. Each page should have exactly one — it anchors the document outline.
Let\'s plant the word Sprout inside a heading. Type it between the opening and closing tags — then press Grow!
Your challenge: write an <h1> containing the word Sprout, then run it.
Task: produce an h1 element whose text content includes \"Sprout\". Validate via the preview.
Write a heading that says Sprout 🌱
Create an <h1> heading with the text Sprout

Tags hug your words:

Sprout

— don\'t forget the closing tag with the slash!

Pattern:

your text

. The closing tag needs a forward slash.

Sprout

Headings are titles, and paragraphs are the stories under them. Paragraphs use the

tag.
Paragraphs hold body text. Combine headings and paragraphs to structure any page.
Use h1–h6 for hierarchy and p for body copy. Semantic structure improves accessibility.
Add a paragraph under your heading that tells everyone about your garden!

Add a

element below your heading with at least one sentence.
Compose a heading plus at least one paragraph element.

Every web page has a secret skeleton: html on the outside, then head and body inside — like bark, branches and leaves!
A full document nests tags: <html> wraps <head> (info) and <body> (content).
Document anatomy: doctype, html root, head metadata, body content. Order and nesting matter.
Stack the blocks to build a whole web page skeleton!
Arrange the blocks into a valid HTML document.
Order the document: doctype → html → head → body, with correct closing order.
Links are magic doorways between pages! The <a> tag makes them, with href telling the door where to go.
The anchor tag <a href=\"…\"> creates links. The href attribute holds the destination.
Anchors define hyperlinks: label. Attributes are name=\"value\" pairs inside the opening tag.
Make a link that says Visit the forest
Create an <a> link with an href attribute
Author an anchor element with a valid href attribute
link text — the href goes inside the opening tag.
href is an attribute of the opening tag, quoted.
The tag plants a picture on your page. It\'s special — it doesn\'t need a closing tag! It needs src (the picture) and alt (words that describe it).
is self-closing. src points to the image; alt describes it for screen readers.
img is a void element. Always provide alt text — it\'s essential for accessibility.
Add a picture tag with src and alt
Write an tag with src and alt attributes
Add an img element with src and alt attributes
— no closing tag needed!
Two attributes on one void element.
Build a <ul> list block by block
Lists keep things tidy, like seeds in a row! <ul> starts the list and every seed sits in an <li>.
Unordered lists: <ul> wraps <li> items. Ordered lists use <ol>.
List semantics: ul/ol containers with li children. Nesting must close in reverse order.
Stack the blocks to grow a list of three plants!
Arrange the blocks into a valid <ul> list.
Construct a valid list — beware of the decoy block.
CSS is the paintbrush of the web! With a style tag you can color your headings any color you like.
CSS styles HTML. Inside <style>, rules look like: h1 { color: green; }
CSS rules: selector { property: value; }. Embed with a style element for now; external sheets later.
Color your heading green with CSS
Use a <style> block to set the h1 color
Add a style element with a color rule applied to h1
<style> h1 { color: green; } </style> — then your <h1> below it!
style block + h1 selector + color property.
selector h1, property color, value of your choice.
Combine everything into a tiny website
Time for your first real creation! Build a page with a heading, a paragraph and a list. Your biome will love it!
Project time: combine a heading, paragraph and a list into one page. This unlocks the Web Gardener badge.
Capstone for this path: heading, paragraph, list, and optional CSS — composed into a single page.
Build a page with a heading, a paragraph and a list
Compose a page containing h1, p and a list structure
Stack them like layers: heading first, then paragraph, then your list!
All three structures, one after another.
h1 + p + ul>li. Optionally add a style block.
Python is a language that talks to computers! The print() spell makes words appear in the console.
Python\'s print() function writes text to the console — it\'s how programs talk back.
print() writes to stdout. Strings are quoted; arguments are comma-separated.
Try making the console say Hello, Meadow! — type your words inside the quotes.
Challenge: print the text Hello, Meadow! exactly.
Make the console say Hello, Meadow!
print(\"Hello, Meadow!\") — quotes hug your words!
print(\"…\") with the message inside quotes.
A single print call with a string literal.
A variable is a little seed box with a name. Put something inside with = and use it later!
Variables store values: plant = \"fern\". Use the name anywhere you need the value.
Assignment binds a name to a value. Names are case-sensitive; no declaration keyword needed.
Make a variable called plant and print it
Create a variable named plant and print its value
Bind plant to a string and print it
plant = \"fern\" then print(plant) — no quotes around the name when printing!
Assignment then a print of the identifier.
Python can do math like a calculator! 3 + 4 makes 7. Words in quotes are called strings.
Numbers support +, -, *, /. Strings are text in quotes; + glues strings together.
Numeric types: int and float. String concatenation with +; mixing types requires str() conversion.
Print the result of 6 * 7 using Python math
Multiplication uses the * operator inside print().
Computers read code like a recipe: top to bottom, one step at a time. If the steps are jumbled, the cake goes wrong!
Execution order matters — a variable must be created before you use it.
Statements execute sequentially. Names must be bound before they\'re referenced.
Put the recipe in order so the plant gets watered!
Order the statements so the program runs without errors.
Sequence the statements respecting data dependencies.
Code can make choices! IF it\'s sunny, water the plants. ELSE, take a nap. The if statement checks, and indented lines belong to it.
if checks a condition; the indented block runs when it\'s true. else handles the other case.
Conditionals: if/elif/else with indentation-defined blocks. Comparison operators: ==, !=, <, >.
Use if/else so the console says grow! when sun is more than 5
Write an if/else that prints grow! when sun > 5
Branch on sun > 5; print grow! in the true case
if sun > 5: then an indented print(\"grow!\") under it. Don\'t forget the colon!
if sun > 5: newline, 4 spaces, print(\"grow!\"), then else: with its own print.
Colon after the condition; consistent 4-space indentation.
Loops repeat things so you don\'t have to! for i in range(3): does its indented lines three times — like three drops of rain.
for i in range(n): repeats the block n times. i counts from 0 to n-1.
for iterates over an iterable; range(n) yields 0..n-1. The loop body is the indented block.
Make it rain! Print drip 3 times with a loop
Use a for loop to print drip three times
for i in range(3): then indented print(\"drip\")
range(3) gives you exactly three repetitions.
Single loop, single print in the body.
Let\'s build a loop out of blocks! Remember: the for line comes first, and the indented lines live inside it.
Assemble a loop with a counter. Watch which lines are indented — they run inside the loop.
Assemble a counting loop. One block is a decoy that would break the program.
Stack the blocks so the garden counts to three!
Order the blocks into a loop that prints 1, 2, 3.
Construct the counter loop; exclude the decoy statement.
Collect many things in one place
A list is a basket that holds many things: seeds = [\"fern\", \"moss\", \"vine\"]. You can loop through the basket too!
Lists hold ordered items: seeds = [\"fern\", \"moss\"]. Loop with: for s in seeds:
Lists are ordered, mutable sequences. Iterate directly: for item in items: …
Make a list of 3 plants and print each one with a loop
Create a list of three items and print each using a for loop
Define a 3-element list and iterate, printing each element
seeds = [\"fern\", \"moss\", \"vine\"] then for s in seeds: and print(s) indented!
List literal with brackets, then for…in, then an indented print.
Name a block of code and reuse it
A function is a recipe with a name! def greet(): saves the steps. Calling greet() runs them — as many times as you like!
def name(): defines a function. Call it with name(). Parameters let you pass values in.
Functions encapsulate behavior: def f(param): … Call with arguments; return sends values back.
Make a function called greet that prints namaste and call it
Define greet() to print namaste, then call it
Define and invoke greet() printing namaste
def greet(): with print(\"namaste\") indented, then greet() on its own line at the end!
Define then call at module level.
Oh no — this code has a sneaky bug! Real coders LOVE finding bugs. Read the error, fix the line and make the garden happy again.
This program crashes. Run it, read the error message, then fix the broken line.
Debugging exercise: run, read the traceback, patch the defect, re-run to verify.
Fix the bug so the code prints harvest time
Fix the error so the program prints harvest time
Repair the defect; expected output: harvest time
Look very closely at the spelling of print — computers need it exactly right!
The function name is misspelled. Python tells you the unknown name.
NameError: identifier typo on the call.
Every HTML element is a box. CSS controls its size, padding and background. Let\'s style a card.
The box model: content, padding, border, margin. Style a container with padding and background-color.
Style a div with a background color and padding using CSS
Apply background-color and padding to a div via a style block
div { background-color: lightgreen; padding: 16px; } inside a style block.
Forms collect input. <form> wraps fields like <input> and a submit <button>.
Forms: form element wrapping labeled inputs and a button. Labels improve accessibility.
Build a form with an input and a button
Compose a form containing an input and a button element
Nest input and button inside form.
Conditions can live inside conditions. Trace the flow carefully before ordering the blocks.
Nested conditionals: indentation depth defines scope. One decoy block included.
Order the nested if/else so the weather report makes sense.
Sequence the nested conditional; exclude the unreachable branch.
Lists have positions starting at 0. seeds[0] is the first item; len(seeds) counts them.
Sequence operations: zero-based indexing, len(), append(). Off-by-one errors live here.
Print the first item and the length of a list
Print element [0] and len() of a list
Compose functions with parameters and return
Functions can take parameters and return results: def double(n): return n * 2. Then print(double(4)).
Parameterized functions with return values compose into pipelines. Build double() and use it.
Write double(n) that returns n * 2 and print double(4)
def double(n): return n * 2 — then print(double(4)) prints 8.
Return, don\'t print, inside the function.
Build a profile card: a heading with your name, a paragraph about you, and CSS to style it. River Builder badge awaits!
Compose a styled profile card: structure plus a style block. Completes the Riverbank path.
Build a card with a heading, paragraph and a style block
Card layout: h1 + p + CSS rules in one page
Combine what you learned: h1, p, and style with background and padding.
Pro editor, workspaces and clean code
Welcome to the Canopy. From here on you\'ll use the professional editor: line numbers, error panel, run history and saved workspaces. Treat every exercise like a real project.
Clean code principles: meaningful names, small functions, no duplication. Your future self is your most important teammate.
APIs let programs talk to each other — conceptually, a menu of requests. Consica Code stays fully offline, but the mental model matters for real-world work.
Real pages are composed of regions: header, main, footer. Build all three with content inside each.
Build a page with header, main and footer sections
Three semantic containers in order, each with content.
Process a list with loops and conditions
Combine a list, a loop, a condition and an accumulator: total rainfall above a threshold. This is the shape of real data processing.
Sum only the values greater than 10 from the list and print the total
Initialize total = 0; loop; if value > 10: total = total + value; print after the loop.
Algorithms are precise sequences. Assemble a working linear search — two decoy blocks will try to sneak in.
Order the linear search; exclude both decoys.
Professional debugging: reproduce, read the error, isolate, fix, verify. This script has two defects — find both.
Fix both bugs so the script prints: average: 20
One typo\'d identifier, one wrong operator. The traceback finds the first; reasoning finds the second.
The capstone: a complete Digital Garden page — title, intro, a list of three projects, and styling. Ship it like a portfolio piece.
Build the full page: heading, paragraph, 3-item list and a style block
Everything from this path, composed deliberately. Take your time.
